A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same E-SUOT research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: v1 reports original GDA and UDA experiments, ablations, sensitivity studies, and transport simulations in the main text and Appendix F.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds baseline evaluations, synthetic transport experiments, and Office-Home discrepancy analyses.

M1.justification: The E-SUOT objectives, sequential potential-then-map optimization, transport chain, and label-preserving classifier adaptation remain unchanged. The added Sinkhorn pseudocode describes a comparison solver, not a new E-SUOT component.

E1.justification: Portraits, MNIST 45/60 degrees, Office-Home, and the existing label-shift scenarios are retained. Sections C.4 and C.6.3 add limited synthetic coverage through transformed two-dimensional Gaussian mixtures and a one-dimensional normal-to-bimodal transport task.

E2.justification: Tables 1 and 2 add MMDSW, SMMD, STDW, and AST to the GDA and UDA comparisons. Appendix F.1 extends the original DSM-based motivation comparison with seven density-estimation approaches, including RealNVP, FM, GKDE, and GMFlow. Section C.4.2 additionally compares Sinkhorn and dual optimization against EMD.

E3.justification: New protocols compare solver runtime, marginal error, and transport cost across sample sizes 50–500; estimate particle KL divergence using a kNN entropy estimator; and evaluate classwise and Gromov-Wasserstein discrepancies on Office-Home. Existing benchmark splits, accuracy metrics, and E-SUOT hyperparameters are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds primal-dual convergence analysis, transport-plan sensitivity to entropy strength, a particle-evolution case study, broader tests of the density-estimation motivation, and geometry-based analysis of negative transfer. The earlier training, UMAP, hyperparameter, early-step, and label-shift ablations remain.

E5.justification: The GDA run description changes from 'five different random seeds at least three times' to 'at least three random seeds'; this does not establish an actual run-count reduction. Uncertainty values disappear from v1 Tables 7–8, retained as v2 Tables 8–9. The sensitivity-plot caption newly identifies its shading as one standard deviation.

E6.justification: Numerous comparator, solver, density-estimation, and discrepancy results are added. STDW becomes runner-up on Portraits and MNIST 60 degrees at 84.3% and 43.9%. E-SUOT retains 86.4%, 72.1%, and 51.0% on the three GDA datasets and 73.5% Office-Home average accuracy. Some Self Train improvement percentages change despite unchanged accuracies.

T1.justification: Proposition 3.2 changes from non-unique dual optima to a Gaussian-mixture statement about non-unique inner c-transform minimizers, with a replacement proof. Proposition 3.4 gains explicit qualifications and potential normalization. Proposition 3.5 adds W2 <= 2 eta and a substantially different proof. Appendix C.7 revises the risk decomposition, summation indices, and statistical bound.

C1.justification: The central density-free semi-dual formulation, entropy-stabilized training, and empirical superiority claims remain. However, v2's conclusion drops the explicit assertion that regularization ensures uniqueness, while the supporting uniqueness and transport-bound statements become qualified.

C2.justification: New interpretations address solver conditioning, entropy-induced smoothing, and why E-SUOT can help or harm strong UDA backbones depending on semantic and structural mismatch. Appendix F.5 explicitly discusses negative transfer. Most label-invariance and training-efficiency limitations already existed and are relocated to Appendix G.

D1.justification: v2 documents new baseline settings, including SMMD/MMDSW kernels, AST's perturbation budget and steps, and STDW's migration steps. It adds solver pseudocode and synthetic-test parameters. Core architecture, optimizer, hardware, and E-SUOT settings remain; the explicit disclosure of reimplementing missing GGF components is shortened.

R1.justification: The cited literature expands across UDA, density estimation, gradient flows, and mathematical foundations. Section 5.2 substantively revises the distinction from Schrödinger-bridge approaches: v1 emphasizes Sinkhorn-based solving, whereas v2 emphasizes an independent product-marginal reference versus a Brownian endpoint reference.

P1.justification: Theoretical derivations and experimental commentary undergo substantial rewriting and explanatory expansion. Sections C.4 and C.6 gain subdivisions, and detailed limitations move to Appendix G, replacing the impact statement. The title spelling, affiliations, publication header, terminology, and numerous references also receive editorial changes.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures 4–8 and Tables 6 and 10, expands the baseline tables, and redraws the runtime comparison with additional methods and a logarithmic axis. Existing motivation panels receive a Figure 1 caption; several retained displays are relocated or renumbered.

improvement.justification: Broader relevant baseline comparisons and the new negative-transfer analysis improve the empirical assessment, while qualified theoretical statements make their scope clearer. These gains are limited by removed uncertainty reporting in retained studies and inconsistencies in the new solver discussion: Table 6 shows much greater dual runtime and marginal error than the primal solver, contrary to parts of Section C.4.2's explanation. The revision therefore provides a modest net improvement, without establishing that its theoretical and reporting deficiencies are resolved.
